Let
\[
\varepsilon_X:A(X)\to \mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon_X\left(\sum_x u_xe_x\right)=\sum_x u_x
\]
be the augmentation map.

Every natural bilinear product is forced by what it does to basis pairs. For distinct \(x,y\), naturality from the two-point set gives
\[
\mu_X(e_x,e_y)=a e_x+b e_y
\]
for fixed integers \(a,b\). For \(x=y\), naturality from a one-point set gives
\[
\mu_X(e_x,e_x)=c e_x.
\]
Now apply the map collapsing two distinct points \(x,y\) to one point. Naturality requires
\[
(a+b)e_z=c e_z,
\]
so \(c=a+b\).

Thus every natural bilinear product has the form
\[
\mu_X(u,v)=a\,\varepsilon_X(v)u+b\,\varepsilon_X(u)v
\]
for fixed integers \(a,b\).

Now impose associativity. Write \(|u|=\varepsilon_X(u)\). Then
\[
(u*v)*w
=a^2|v||w|u+ab|u||w|v+b(a+b)|u||v|w,
\]
while
\[
u*(v*w)
=a(a+b)|v||w|u+ab|u||w|v+b^2|u||v|w.
\]
These are equal for all \(u,v,w\) iff
\[
ab=0.
\]

Therefore the associative natural bilinear products are exactly
\[
\boxed{\mu_X(u,v)=\lambda\,\varepsilon_X(v)u\quad\text{for some }\lambda\in\mathbb Z}
\]
or
\[
\boxed{\mu_X(u,v)=\lambda\,\varepsilon_X(u)v\quad\text{for some }\lambda\in\mathbb Z.}
\]
The zero product occurs in both families when \(\lambda=0\).
